common.title: Your cell chooses where to swim
common.text: Build organs to shape what your cell can sense and do. It chooses when to feed, hunt, escape or seek light; you do not steer it directly.

common.title: Choose overlapping structures
common.text: When several structures share a spot, choose the one you want from the temporary selection menu. Its pictures match the factories, organs and stores on your cell; damaged organs have a pink ring.

common.title: Build and restore
common.text: Open Assembly for movement, oral grooves, armor and glands, Chemistry for internal organs and leaves, or Receptors for free chemical senses. The first two non-receptor organelles on each cell are free. After those, prices follow Fibonacci ×10: 10, 10, 20, 30, 50, 80… biomass. Reabsorbing one moves the next build back one step. Free receptors do not advance the sequence. Both starter organelles can be replaced.

common.title: Read the cell’s resources
common.text: Biomass builds and repairs your cell. ATP powers its work. Construction shows its biomass price before you place it. Free construction does not mean free running costs.

common.title: Reabsorb and specialize
common.text: Open an organelle and choose Reabsorb to remove it. Half its remaining paid tissue returns as biomass. A free build returns no biomass. Adaptations change matching organelles; free division mutation offers appear in the nucleus.

common.title: Choose adaptations
common.text: Open the nucleus to keep an offered division mutation. Open a matching organelle to apply a learned mutation. Photosynthesis always offers Sun or Shade: Sun seeks brighter water; Shade seeks soft light and turns toward light if it is too dark. These choices are free.

common.title: Understand your cell’s instincts
common.text: Intent view starts on. Nucleus → Instinct toggles the live intention readout and direction arrow. Low ATP favors food, useful light or resting while food digests. Low biomass favors feeding or hunting. Healthy cells can hunt or explore. Harmful acid and attacks take priority; family traces help attacked cells spread out. The same instincts apply to every cell, using its own organs and local signals.

common.title: Cell division
common.text: Open Divide and choose Mitosis or Budding. Mitosis leaves your organelles with the parent and uses half your available biomass to grow a basic daughter. Budding funds a small daughter directly. Neither needs clear water. Each cell can reproduce once per minute. Both automatic modes start on and let instincts choose suitable moments. At 12 family members, an extra daughter is immediately reabsorbed.

common.title: View your family
common.text: Nucleus → Family shows all living relatives together as pictures of their current cells. The tiny corner number is each cell’s generation. Choose a living relative to manage it; your previous cell stays alive. The menu grows to fit your screen; scroll if your family needs more room. The header keeps the highest generation and lifetime cell count. Deceased relatives leave the list.

common.title: Pause and personalize
common.text: Pause freezes your view while the pond continues. Resume returns to the live world with one press. Pause includes Gameplay, Mechanics, feedback, music, your family name and a first name for your favorite cell.

common.title: Start a new lineage
common.text: In Pause, choose Start new lineage and confirm. Your former family stays alive in the pond under computer control; you begin with a new cell. This does not reset the shared pond. Wait a minute before starting another.

common.title: Smooth camera changes
common.text: Following, recentering, changing views and switching family members glide into place. Pause holds the camera; direct camera gestures stay responsive. Nearby water is prepared ahead of your view to reduce empty patches while exploring.

common.title: Choose unattended investments
common.text: Open the nucleus or Divide, then Invest. Manual is the default. Choose Hunter, Producer or Grazer, or save a relative’s current build as an example. Unattended cells use their own biomass and make at most one build or reabsorption per minute. Family settings and individual exceptions are separate. The family controls also switch automatic mitosis and budding.

common.title: Choose your lineage color
common.text: Pause → Lineage color opens a color disc. Drag around the outer ring to change hue. Drag across the inner disc for saturation and brightness, then Save color. The choice applies to your lineage and stays after reconnecting.

common.title: Your favorite cell
common.text: Your last directly selected relative gets a gold outline. When you are offline, paused or the game tab is hidden, it cannot die, lose organs or be automatically absorbed. Its biomass and ATP can still run out. It becomes vulnerable when you return to active play.

touch.title: Move, turn and zoom
touch.text: Use two fingers together: drag to move the view, twist to rotate, and pinch to zoom. The touched places stay under your fingers. The + and − buttons also zoom.

touch.title: Follow and look inside
touch.text: Tap Follow to center on your cell. Tap Internal to look inside, or External to return to the pond. Inside, gestures stay relative to your cell and you can zoom much closer. Returning outside keeps your zoom within the pond view limits.

touch.title: Open cell controls
touch.text: Tap a factory, nucleus, growing bud, ATP store or installed organelle. Choices appear along the top. Tap × or empty water to close choices.

touch.title: Cancel placement
touch.text: Tap the circular icon of the held organelle at the top left to cancel placing it.

touch.title: Switch family member
touch.text: Double-tap a living cell in your lineage to manage it. Your previous cell stays in the pond.

touch.title: Inspect particles
touch.text: Tap a particle or vacuole to see its name and details at the bottom.

touch.title: Show resources
touch.text: Biomass and ATP appear along the bottom. Tap − to hide them and Resources to bring them back.

touch.title: Pause, resume and music
touch.text: Tap Pause for the menu and Resume to return to the live view. Tap Enable music when shown, then Music to mute or resume; the slider changes volume.

touch.title: Family and growth
touch.text: Tap Family to switch relatives. Merge zooms to nearby water: tap a bright relative to merge it into your current cell immediately. You do not need to travel to it. Only unattended relatives whose pheromones your cell received within the past five seconds are selectable; other cells are dim. Tap Cancel merge to leave. Swipe through long families, or use the up/down arrows. Open the division bud, then Divide for continuous Auto divide or a single queued birth. Investment shows all three strategies and whether this cell uses Family or an individual setting.

desktop.title: Move and zoom
desktop.text: Scroll the mouse wheel to zoom. Drag with the middle mouse button to pan in Free view or inside a cell. In Free view, dragging empty water with the left button also pans.

desktop.title: Follow and look inside
desktop.text: Space toggles Follow / Free view outside the cell and recenters the cell frame inside. I switches Internal / External.

desktop.title: Open cell controls
desktop.text: Click a factory, nucleus, growing bud, ATP store or organelle. Tab enters or leaves cell editing.

desktop.title: Cancel placement
desktop.text: Right-click cancels a held organelle or closes choices. Clicking the held icon also cancels.

desktop.title: Build with the keyboard
desktop.text: [ and ] cycle cell targets; Enter opens the selected target or places the held organelle. Arrow keys adjust choices or membrane placement. Number keys and F / C / V select organelle types. R opens the new-lineage confirmation.

desktop.title: Switch family member
desktop.text: Double-click a living cell in your lineage, or choose it from the family menu. Your previous cell stays in the pond.

desktop.title: Inspect and inspect more
desktop.text: Hover over a particle for its name and magnified shape. Hold Alt for expanded cell and organelle details.

desktop.title: Pause, settings and display
desktop.text: P pauses or resumes your view. M opens or closes settings. F11 toggles fullscreen. S toggles sensed signals; F3 toggles the information overlay. Music and resource controls are in the cell and Pause menu.

desktop.title: Family and growth
desktop.text: Click Family to switch relatives. Merge zooms to nearby water: click a bright relative to merge it into your current cell immediately. You do not need to travel to it. Only unattended relatives whose pheromones your cell received within the past five seconds are selectable; other cells are dim. Right-click or use Cancel merge to leave. Use the up/down arrows to scroll long families. Open the division bud, then Divide for continuous Auto divide or a single queued birth. Investment shows all three strategies and whether this cell uses Family or an individual setting.

items.title: Food → ATP, biomass and waste
items.text: The oral groove takes in real food particles. Food vacuoles drift inside for at least 10 seconds while digesting their contents. ATP and biomass are stored amounts; waste-filled vacuoles move to the outlet and are expelled.

sources.title: How cells obtain energy from food

items.title: Food + oxygen → more useful energy
items.text: Nearby oxygen supports more efficient digestion and more biomass. Without enough oxygen, fermentation still processes food but yields less. Carbon and waste are released. These are simplified food-processing rules, not full molecular pathways.

sources.title: How cells obtain energy from food

items.title: Carbon + light → food, biomass and oxygen
items.text: Leaves use dissolved CO2 and light to make food, biomass, oxygen and ATP. Air slowly replenishes carbon throughout the pond, with excess carbon returning to the air near a low local saturation. One healthy leaf can sustain a basic cell even in dim water; larger active builds need more leaves and efficient respiration. Sun and Shade still favor different light conditions. Most new food stays inside, with a little released into the pond. Attacks and damaging acid can still kill a cell.

sources.title: Gas exchange between air and water

items.title: Emergency fuel
items.text: Below 12 ATP, cells can burn stored biomass directly for a modest ATP yield until they recover to 18 ATP. This spends their reserves and can eventually lead to starvation; it does not create a fresh meal.

items.title: ATP pays for work
items.text: Maintenance, swimming, pumping, repair and secretion spend ATP. Ordinary light collection and sensing remain possible at zero ATP. Free receptors need no biomass to repair; repair still uses ATP.

items.title: Low ATP: quarter capacity
items.text: Low ATP slows movement, feeding currents, glands and active repair to 25% capacity instead of switching them off. Weapons recharge four times more slowly. Normal activity returns automatically when ATP recovers. Organs still need their usual materials and signals. Digestion, photosynthesis, sensing and passive protection keep their existing operation. This residual capacity is a game rule.

items.title: Particles have to meet
items.text: Chemical parcels drift, turn and mix with the water. Reactions need compatible contact and facing. They stand for amounts of material, not individual molecules.

items.title: Nutrient + nutrient → a richer parcel
items.text: Joining combines the food. Fully fueled parcels also gain a bounded ATP-yield bonus. Mild acid helps them bind; joining spent food does not refill its energy. The bonus is a game rule inspired by pH-sensitive assembly.

items.title: Enzyme + waste → reusable food
items.text: An aligned digestive enzyme converts waste into edible material and can be reused. Moderate acidity helps; too much prevents the reaction. Recycling does not restore the food’s spent fuel.

items.title: Waste + oxygen → food and carbon
items.text: When conditions permit, oxygen helps turn waste into reusable food material and carbon. Recycled food has no fresh fuel. This contact rule stands in for wider microbial reabsorption, rather than a literal chemical equation.

items.title: Antitoxin + toxin, tag or pore part → waste
items.text: A neutralizer binds an attacking parcel and makes harmless waste containing both parcels’ material. Real antitoxins are specific; the game combines several defenses into one.

items.title: Toxin + nutrient → waste
items.text: Toxins spoil food they contact. The toxin remains dangerous. This is a game simplification of contamination.

items.title: Acid + buffer → spent charge
items.text: Acid raises local acidity; buffers reduce it. Opposite charges neutralize each other, and exhausted parcels become waste. Pink water shows acidity; the colors are an aid, not a real pH scale.

items.title: Waste, carbon or oxygen + matching parcel → a larger parcel
items.text: Matching parcels can combine up to their size limit, keeping their material. Only nutrient binding has the extra ATP-yield rule.

items.title: Toxin + cell → damage
items.text: Toxin packets can hurt any cell they reach, including relatives and their source. A neutralizer can intercept them. Defense and repair compete with the attacker’s finite supplies.

items.title: Tag + membrane + four pore parts → a damaging pore
items.text: Surface tags attach locally. Pore parts land at the same small patch and build from a curved piece through a crescent and open ring. Four complete an active pore on the outside of the membrane. Antitoxin can cap an unfinished assembly, while repair helps remove an active pore. The four-part recipe is fictional. Free tags and subunits disperse quickly, keeping attacks local. Pieces already attached to a membrane keep assembling.

items.title: Decoy + receptor → weaker sensing
items.text: Decoys temporarily occupy receptors, including those of relatives. They can release on their own; ATP and repair help clear them sooner. Light seeking is separate.

items.title: Pheromones carry old reports
items.text: Hunting and flight receptors read drifting reports of nearby cells. Reports age and expire; they do not reveal another cell’s live location. Family signatures help relatives recognize one another. Hunters still choose non-family targets, but stray toxin, pores and decoys can affect relatives.

items.title: Particles decay and disperse
items.text: Parcels have limited lifetimes. Above the pond’s particle limit, excess exterior parcels have the same chance of dispersing, regardless of type. The limit is a game rule; it never removes cells or their internal contents.

items.title: Flagellum
items.text: Provides propulsion along its mounted axis. Cells respond quickly to thrust and local water without heavy coasting. Larger cells face more drag. Particle movement is unchanged.

items.title: Cilia
items.text: Beat to swim and draw water past the cell. The current carries food and hazards alike; the oral groove still has to take food in.

items.title: Protective cortex
items.text: Protects the patch of membrane beneath it. Coverage depends on placement.

items.title: Oral groove
items.text: An optional mouth on the membrane, built in Assembly. It draws surrounding water toward its opening, takes in food and releases digestive enzymes. A taut internal strand connects the mouth to the center of the cell. Reabsorb it to remove the mouth and strand; leaves and gas uptake still work without it.

items.title: Hunting receptor
items.text: Free Hunting receptors follow any detected non-family pheromone report, regardless of size or defenses. Glands provide the attack.

items.title: Flight receptor
items.text: Free Flight receptors steer away from nearby toxin particles and armed non-family cells detected through pheromones. An unarmed cell’s size alone does not trigger flight.

items.title: Photosynthesis
items.text: Uses light and carbon. Sun leaves seek brighter water; Shade leaves seek soft light, returning toward light when it is too dark. Choose Sun or Shade from its menu.

items.title: Toxin gland
items.text: Spends biomass and ATP to send toxin and receptor-blocking decoys toward a locally reported target.

items.title: Pore-forming gland
items.text: Releases tags and pore parts toward a local target report. Damage requires assembly on an actual membrane, including a relative’s.

items.title: Acid gland
items.text: Releases acid parcels. Mild acid helps food binding and enzyme action, but too much also harms the secreting cell.

items.title: Toxin neutralizer
items.text: Releases antitoxin when a nearby chemical threat is present.

items.title: Buffer / repair gland
items.text: Uses biomass and ATP to repair damage, helps remove pores and decoys, and releases buffer when needed.

items.title: Mitochondrion
items.text: Sits inside the cell and helps recover more ATP from food and nearby oxygen without reducing biomass growth. Each healthy mitochondrion adds 50% to ordinary oxygen-supported digestion: one gives 1.5x ATP, two give 2x, up to 5x. Damage reduces its benefit. It has a small upkeep cost. Direct leaf ATP and fermentation are unchanged; exhausted food cannot make extra energy.

items.title: Counterattack gland
items.text: Fires at the last position reported by a nearby chemical warning from an armed cell. Its toxin spares cells without offensive organs. Perfect sparing is a game rule inspired by local bacterial counterattack.

items.title: Toxin sac
items.text: Stores toxin slowly from surplus biomass, using ATP while filling. A fuller sac has a larger pink center. When its cell dies, the stored toxin spills into nearby water as ordinary toxin particles. Reabsorbing safely dismantles it. It gives no new senses or suicidal behavior. This defensive organelle and its quantities are game choices.

sources.title: Toxin accumulation and release by cell lysis

items.title: Toward family receptor
items.text: A free receptor from the purple Receptor factory. Steers toward locally detected family pheromone trails. Food, energy recovery and danger take priority. It needs movement organs to swim; it cannot locate relatives that it has not sensed.

items.title: Away from family receptor
items.text: A free receptor from the purple Receptor factory. Steers away from locally detected family pheromone trails, helping relatives spread out. Survival needs take priority. Free receptors do not raise the next organelle’s price and return no paid biomass when reabsorbed.

items.title: Biomass, shape and support
items.text: Biomass supports growth and repair. The membrane deforms around a lightly drawn internal support network. That network is sampled per cell and is not editable.

items.title: Mitosis and budding
items.text: Mitosis and budding use available biomass and ATP directly, with no investment bank. Mitosis keeps the parent’s organs and splits its biomass budget and remaining ATP. Budding pays for a small daughter. Daughters begin with a leaf and removable oral groove, inherit investment choices, and wait a minute before reproducing. Families keep at most 12 cells through immediate reabsorption.

sources.title: Cell division
sources.text: Open Divide and choose Mitosis or Budding. Mitosis leaves your organelles with the parent and uses half your available biomass to grow a basic daughter. Budding funds a small daughter directly. Neither needs clear water. Each cell can reproduce once per minute. Both automatic modes start on and let instincts choose suitable moments. At 12 family members, an extra daughter is immediately reabsorbed.

items.title: Mutations and inheritance
items.text: Each completed birth has a 10% chance to offer a free mutation in the nucleus. Daughters inherit investment settings, not copies of the parent’s organelles. They start with a removable oral groove and leaf.

sources.title: Cell division
sources.text: Open Divide and choose Mitosis or Budding. Mitosis leaves your organelles with the parent and uses half your available biomass to grow a basic daughter. Budding funds a small daughter directly. Neither needs clear water. Each cell can reproduce once per minute. Both automatic modes start on and let instincts choose suitable moments. At 12 family members, an extra daughter is immediately reabsorbed.

items.title: Hunger is gradual
items.text: Low ATP can draw on spare reserves and biomass. Prolonged serious shortage eventually damages the cell; brief shortages have a grace period. Feeding, photosynthesis and repair can help it recover.

items.title: Death returns material to the pond
items.text: A dying cell ruptures and releases its remaining represented contents. The material can feed other cells; the attacker receives no private food reward.

sources.title: Release of contents when cells rupture

items.title: The pond continues
items.text: Cells keep living while players are away. Updates preserve saved cells and accounts. The main and experimental ponds have separate cells and progress. If your lineage is lost, a new cell brings you back; the pond keeps a minimum of 15 living cells and restarts if completely empty. These are game rules.

items.title: Contractile vacuoles
items.text: The paired pulsing structures and canals illustrate water regulation. They do not currently simulate osmotic water balance or create resources.

items.title: Other cells develop too
items.text: Manual investment is the default. Opt into Hunter, Producer, Grazer or a saved relative’s build for unattended development. A cell can spend biomass or reabsorb an unsuitable organelle once per minute. Family defaults and individual choices are both available.

items.title: Currents and plants
items.text: Broad currents carry cells and chemical parcels through the pond. Swimming adds movement relative to the local water; leftover cell motion quickly settles back into that current. Feeding stirs the water locally. Plants damp flow; cells meet plant branches while chemistry can pass through. This is a stylized fluid world, not a calibrated microscopic-water model.

items.title: Changing conditions
items.text: Bright turquoise water and deep shade form broad, soft-edged patches. Rippling light shimmers in the sunlit water. Conditions also vary with the calendar and time of day, changing roughly hourly. Brighter water supports photosynthesis; excessive acid is stressful. The pattern and schedule are game choices.

items.title: Inside and outside views
items.text: External shows exterior chemistry. Internal focuses on the followed cell’s contents and dims the exterior. The rest of the pond keeps evolving.

items.title: Identity and music
items.text: Names appear above player lineages and brighten while their owner is connected. Music responds to the world, but muting it does not change the cell’s biology. Pause also lets you choose your lineage’s color. Color and readiness rings are visual aids; they do not change biology.

items.title: Gentle eddies and currents
items.text: Spiral eddies and directional currents move around the pond at 10–50 µm/s. Each lasts 1–20 seconds and spans 30–100 µm. Events overlap so there is always one stirring the water. Plants soften passing currents, with half their previous damping. A short golden stretch marks water immediately around an induced current source; ordinary trails keep their usual color. These are simplified game currents.

sources.title: External forces that drive water currents

items.title: Shared instincts, different bodies
items.text: Intent view starts on. Nucleus → Instinct toggles the current intention and direction arrow on or off. This only changes what you see. All cells escape harm, recover ATP, rebuild biomass, then hunt or explore using their actual organs and locally received chemical, light and acidity signals. Unattended relatives can follow family traces to merge; crowding makes this more likely.

items.title: Air, CO2 and oxygen
items.text: CO2 enters the water gradually from the air. A much smaller amount of oxygen also dissolves from air; leaves produce oxygen through photosynthesis. Faster-moving water exchanges gases faster, with a small background exchange in still water. The gases remain real moving parcels that must reach the cell. Saturation levels, parcel sizes and the use of fluid speed as a surface-mixing cue are game choices.

items.title: Merging relatives
items.text: Choose an unattended relative through Family after receiving its pheromone within the last five seconds. The merge happens immediately, and its image briefly slides into your cell. Resources combine once. Cells do not randomly merge below the family limit. Extra births beyond 12 are immediately reabsorbed into their parent.

items.title: Acid can help—and harm
items.text: Mild acidity helps nutrients join and digestive enzymes recycle waste. Joined food can deliver a larger share of its existing fuel as ATP; spent food cannot be refueled this way. Excess acid costs ATP and damages cells. Buffer/repair glands respond to harmful exposure, protecting the cell without immediately erasing useful mild acidity. Water tint and reaction flashes show the chemistry.

items.title: Roles come from anatomy
items.text: A leafless cell with a hunting receptor, flagellum and attack gland becomes a Hunter: quicker, cheaper movement and protection from its own pore parts. Two working leaves and a mitochondrion, with no weapons or mouth, make a Producer: stronger photosynthesis and a firm, boxy cell wall. An oral groove and cilia without leaves or weapons make a Grazer with greater intake and ATP recovery. Only one role bonus applies. These are simplified game bonuses.

items.title: Crowding and autolysis
items.text: Unattended, unprotected cells that keep receiving signals from more than six relatives have a small chance to break down and return their contents. A family cannot trigger this more than once per minute. Chemical reports are the only crowding information. The numerical probabilities are game rules.

items.title: Growing beyond membrane support
items.text: Above 3,000 total organic material, a cell can develop a temporary tear and leak stored material. Protection organs increase the supported amount. The tear closes after the excess is relieved. This is recoverable stress, not a hard biomass limit.

items.title: Two free organelles
items.text: Each cell has two reusable free construction places, excluding the always-free sensing receptors. The starter leaf and oral groove fill both. Reabsorption returns half of biomass actually paid into an organ; free tissue gives no biomass refund. Free construction material is an explicit game allowance.
